messages.content: Write an internal post about making security everyone's responsibility at a software company. Around 250 words.

**Security isn't AppSec's problem to carry alone**

Four people work in AppSec. About 210 of us write code that ships. Their review queue runs six days deep, and that has nothing to do with effort.

Hiring won't fix the math. Double the team and the queue drops to three days — but a three-day queue teaches the same lesson a six-day one does: file the ticket at the end, hope, ship anyway.

So we're changing where the work lives.

Threat modeling moves into the design doc. No separate template, no sign-off gate. Add a section: what would someone attack here, and what stops them. Fifteen minutes at a whiteboard, written up by whoever owns the doc. AppSec reads those sections instead of authoring them.

Every service gets a named owner responsible for its dependencies, its secret rotation, and its auth handling. "The platform team" doesn't count. A person's name in the service catalog does.

We're also publishing the five worst things that have actually gone wrong here since 2024 — real incidents, redacted only where legal requires it. Generic training slides fade in a week. "Remember the open S3 bucket in March" doesn't.

When you find something, in your code or anyone else's or a vendor's, say so quickly and out loud. No one at this company has ever been penalized for finding a hole. The only wrong move is noticing and staying quiet.

Then four people can do what four people are actually good at: thinking hard about the genuinely hard designs, and building guardrails the rest of us inherit for free. A checkpoint people learn to dodge protects nothing.

**Security isn't something four people can carry**

AppSec is four people. Roughly 210 of us ship code. Their review queue sits six days deep, and effort has nothing to do with it.

The math doesn't yield to hiring. Double the team, get a three-day queue — and a three-day queue teaches exactly what a six-day one does: file the ticket last, cross your fingers, ship anyway.

So the work is moving to where the code is.

Threat modeling goes in the design doc. No separate template, no sign-off gate. Just a section: what would someone attack here, and what stops them. Fifteen minutes at a whiteboard, written down by whoever owns the doc. AppSec reads those sections rather than writing them.

Every service gets a named owner on the hook for its dependencies, its secret rotation, its auth handling. "The platform team" is not an answer. A human name in the service catalog is.

We're also publishing the five worst things that have actually gone wrong here since 2024 — real incidents, redacted only where legal makes us. Generic training slides evaporate in a week. "Remember the open S3 bucket in March" sticks.

Find something — your code, someone else's, a vendor's — and say so fast and in public. Nobody here has ever been punished for finding a hole. The only wrong move is spotting one and going quiet.

Then four people get to do what four people are genuinely good at: chewing on the hard designs, and building guardrails the rest of us get for free. A checkpoint people learn to route around protects nothing.
